entries.subject: One deep mine cutaway, long shaft and three stacked gallery levels, surface hoist subordinate.
entries.prompt:
Use case: precise-object-edit.
Asset type: ONE revised TECHNOLOGY icon for the Victoria 3 1776 mod, not a flat production-method pictogram.
Image 1: EDIT TARGET. Change the concept described below, preserving its hand-painted volumetric material style, natural warm-neutral colors, fine matte brushwork and modest three-quarter viewpoint.
Backdrop: genuine transparent alpha around the isolated composition. No painted black, white, checkerboard, scene background, UI frame, medallion, text, letters, numbers, arrows, logos or watermarks. No ground cast shadow.
Composition: square at least 1024 pixels, full coherent subject within generous transparent margins. One dominant conceptual assembly. Broad masses readable at 48 and 64 px, not photorealistic, glossy 3D, flat vector or fantasy. No global blue/teal cast.
Primary request: the previous icon reads merely as a pithead well. Make DEEP UNDERGROUND MINING unmistakable by replacing the dominant above-ground trestle with a compact, tall ROCK CROSS-SECTION that reveals a deep VERTICAL MINE SHAFT and THREE HORIZONTAL GALLERY LEVELS below one another.
The lower roughly three quarters of the icon are one cohesive narrow warm-grey/brown rough rock slice, shown as an isolated conceptual cutaway sample, not a broad landscape. A single long central cut shaft descends nearly to the bottom. Three distinctly separated dark horizontal galleries branch from it at upper, middle and deep lower levels. Large legible voids, not tiny maze tunnels. Each gallery intersects the same main shaft; nothing floats independently. Visible brown timber props and crossbeams support the exposed gallery mouths and shaft. Limit to a few bold timber members per level; not a dense ladder forest.
At the top, a SMALL simplified wooden hoist with one pulley indicates surface extraction, occupying only the top quarter; keep its wooden and iron vocabulary from Image 1, but reduce it drastically relative to the depth below. One continuous hoisting rope passes over the surface pulley and descends through the long shaft to one small bucket near the deepest level. The vertical rope and lowest bucket draw the eye down and convey depth.
Add a thin simple brown wooden ladder inside one side of the shaft with its rungs aligned, connected to level platforms; no modern cage or rail machinery. Rock is geological supporting material, not a mountain landscape. Natural dark seams in rock remain subordinate to galleries.
One integrated cutaway mine concept with all three levels plainly visible. Do not keep the big standalone pithead as the main subject; no merely taller tower. No buildings, trees, sky, soil landscape, people, electric fan, locomotive, coal pile, decorative props, labels, arrows or black square backdrop. The shaft section is deliberately simplified, historically informed by eighteenth-century mine-section engravings, not a certified technical scale model.
entries.original_prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept.
Asset type: ONE TECHNOLOGY invention icon for the 1776 Age of Revolutions Victoria 3 mod. NOT a production-method pictogram and NOT a building scene.
Style/medium: compact original vanilla-like Victoria 3 hand-painted volumetric object illustration. Broad readable material masses, restrained brushed texture, soft natural shading on objects, coherent three-dimensional construction. Readable at 48 and 64 pixels. Not photorealistic, glossy 3D, flat vector, all-gold icon, miniature landscape or steampunk fantasy.
Backdrop: genuine transparent alpha surrounding the entire object and in all exterior openings. No black/white painted background, checkerboard, room, scenery, ground, floor, cast ground shadow, frame, circle, medallion or badge.
Composition: centered square canvas at least 1024 pixels, all parts intact, generous transparent margins at least ten percent, modest three-quarter view. ONE dominant functional assembly, at most one meaningful subordinate accessory. No disconnected shafts, floating loose parts or impossible connections.
Lighting/palette: soft upper-left illumination. Natural brown timber, warm-neutral grey/dark iron, muted brass and material-specific neutral colors. NO overall blue or teal cast, neon or uniform sepia. Fine fasteners subordinate to a strong silhouette.
Constraints: no people, text, lettering, numbers, arrows, labels, logos or watermark. No electric motor, plastic, power cord, modern control panel or modern safety equipment. Historical conceptual illustration, not a certified engineering reconstruction.
Primary request: DEEP MINE ENGINEERING represented by a compact late-eighteenth/early-nineteenth-century TIMBER PITHEAD HOIST, informed by a 1794 coal-mine winding diagram in the Musée Carnavalet. Not a steel modern mine tower, mine landscape, or merely a pickaxe.
One sturdy brown wooden headframe with two front upright posts, a high transverse crossbeam, and two visibly connected diagonal rear braces. The posts hold a single broad grooved iron sheave on a horizontal axle at the top. A stout rope runs from an integral wooden winding drum low at the rear-left, upward along one side to pass OVER the top sheave, then descends vertically in the open centre. The rope must visibly follow this one continuous winding path.
At the end of the descending rope, ONE small dark iron-bound wooden ore bucket with a rigid curved bail hangs between the posts, just above a short timber collar framing the shaft opening. The bucket is the sole supporting accessory; only a few dark coal lumps inside. The shaft collar is structural timber only with transparent empty centre, NOT a slab of landscape or an earth cutaway.
The rear winding drum is supported by its own short stout bearings attached to the same timber assembly; its handle and axle are connected, not floating. Simplify to one rope, one sheave, one bucket, one drum. No secondary pulley chain, ladder, locomotive, steam engine, gears pile, miners, ventilation fan, large mine building or modern steel wire headframe. Show timber joinery and load-bearing supports with plausible contacts. Strong silhouette rather than an intricate miniature.

entries.subject:
Primary request: MINING SAFETY represented by ONE early DAVY MINER'S SAFETY LAMP, inspired by the Science Museum's gauze lamp made in 1820. The lamp is the entire subject; no pickaxe, helmet, coal pile, decorative shield or extra props.
A squat round muted-brass oil reservoir at the bottom, wider than the vertical cylinder above. A tall DARK IRON FINE WIRE-GAUZE CYLINDER rises from the reservoir, capped with a subtly domed mesh top. Three or four simple straight dark iron guard rods connect the reservoir rim to the top ring. A single sturdy suspension ring centred above the top connects to a small hooked metal loop. Ring opening genuinely transparent.
A tiny warm restrained oil-wick flame is barely visible INSIDE THE LOWER PART of the protective mesh, above the reservoir, contained entirely by it. The wire mesh is the functional flame-arresting enclosure, drawn as subtle grain/cross-hatch rather than harsh moiré. The outline of the dark mesh remains clearly readable against both light and dark backgrounds. Brass rim catches warm-neutral soft light.
No glass chimney, no large exposed torch flame, no magical glow around the object, no electric miner's lamp, no battery, no headlamp, no shiny ornate lantern, no long top chimney, no display pedestal or museum glass dome. This must read as a functional simple early gauze safety lamp rather than a domestic kerosene lantern.

entries.subject: Original air-heating apparatus retained, chamber surfaces visibly red-hot.
entries.prompt:
Use case: precise-object-edit.
Asset type: ONE revised TECHNOLOGY icon for the Victoria 3 1776 mod, not a flat production-method pictogram.
Image 1: EDIT TARGET. Change the concept described below, preserving its hand-painted volumetric material style, natural warm-neutral colors, fine matte brushwork and modest three-quarter viewpoint.
Backdrop: genuine transparent alpha around the isolated composition. No painted black, white, checkerboard, scene background, UI frame, medallion, text, letters, numbers, arrows, logos or watermarks. No ground cast shadow.
Composition: square at least 1024 pixels, full coherent subject within generous transparent margins. One dominant conceptual assembly. Broad masses readable at 48 and 64 px, not photorealistic, glossy 3D, flat vector or fantasy. No global blue/teal cast.
Primary request: the metal in the previous icon looks cold and the heat is not readable. Keep the SAME rectangular iron AIR-HEATING CHAMBER, connected inlet and outlet, brick hearth, integral rear chimney, overall proportions and composition. CHANGE THE TEMPERATURE APPEARANCE OF THE CHAMBER ITSELF so it is visibly INCANDESCENT RED-HOT METAL, not only lit by a fire below.
The large flat rectangular metal chamber is now the dominant hot mass: strong dull cherry-red along cooler upper edges, intense orange-red across its broad lower front plate and lower side plate, with a small bright orange centre nearest the heat below. Make the hot metal unmistakable even at 48/64 pixels. Preserve seams and rivets as darker iron details; retain a few subdued grey/black cooler structural bands at the top so it remains solid iron, not a floating luminous plastic box. The metal is SOLID and has retained its shape; do not melt it into lava or put liquid inside.
Continue the red-hot color softly onto the base of the connected right outlet where it joins the chamber, grading to cooler grey near its tip. Left inlet remains mostly grey. Keep the chamber continuously supported on the same brick hearth and retain the burning coal below, but the coal must not be the ONLY incandescent element.
Heat emission belongs to the metal surfaces only; nearby bricks receive restrained warm reflected light, not an orange wash across everything. No external magical halo, smoke, huge new flames, sparks, molten spill, extra crucible or glowing arrows. No steam fittings, pressure gauge, water, boiler tubes, extra props or letters.
Preserve genuine alpha, isolated three-quarter view, original natural brick material and chimney's proper connection down into the hearth. This is a clearer conceptual heat cue, not a temperature-calibrated museum reconstruction.

Primary request: HOT BLAST SMELTING represented by an early NEILSON AIR PREHEATER inspired by the 1829 wrought-iron heating chamber reproduced in Thomas Turner's Metallurgy of Iron. Show the separate apparatus which heats AIR before it reaches a blast furnace, NOT a steam boiler, water-tube boiler, modern Cowper tower or an entire ironworks.
One compact horizontal rectangular grey wrought-iron AIR CHAMBER, with flat plates and restrained dark riveted seams, mounted within an integral low red-brown BRICK HEARTH. Deliberately show an open-front explanatory cutaway of the brick enclosure, keeping the iron chamber clearly dominant and intact. A small lower arched firing opening shows subdued orange coal heat immediately BELOW the chamber; hot combustion gas surrounds the outside of the chamber, not the inside air passage. Brick supports genuinely meet and support the iron chamber.
One short thick neutral-grey iron inlet pipe joins the LEFT end of the chamber. A distinct connected outlet pipe leaves the RIGHT end and projects forward-right into one simple tapered blast nozzle, all one coherent apparatus. The inlet and outlet must have visible proper connections into opposite ends of the AIR chamber. No disconnected pipes and no water tank or boiler fittings. A very restrained warm reflected highlight on the right outlet suggests heated air; do not draw water, blue vapour or theatrical flames from the nozzle.
A short square brick flue rises directly from the REAR corner of the same brick hearth, with a continuous masonry connection down to the fire enclosure, not a detached chimney. Keep it subordinate to the box and air conduit; no towering factory chimney or visible billowing smoke.
Use a compact natural-grey metal and red-brown brick silhouette, emphatic visible connected air path and fire-under-chamber relationship. No pressure gauge, steam release valve, flywheel, steam piston, boiler drum, U-tube forest, enormous furnace stack, glass tube, electricity or lettering. This is a simplified conceptual cutaway of the first air-heating principle, not a claim of an exact full-scale historical reconstruction.
